To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Fermilab 750 MeV Linac has been tested at peak currents of 85 mA and pulse lengths of up to 50 μsec without significant damage to the Linac.
the Fermilab 400 MeV H Linac can accelerate H beam with peak currents up to 85 mA with beam losses comparable to present Linac operation.
we have shown that the Fermilab 800 MeV Linac can accelerate H beam at a peak current of ~100 mA with a pulse length of ~100 μsec.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of high current beams in the Fermilab 800 MeV Proton Linac.
the development and operation of a high current, high power, proton accelerator.
the development of a high intensity proton driver for the next generation of neutrino oscillation experiments and the design of an accelerator for a muon collider.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Linac can be operated with a peak beam current up to ~100 mA.
the Linac has a peak current of ~100 mA with a 50 μsec pulse length.
the present Linacs are not capable of accelerating beam at the required current and pulse lengths for a proton driver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the present Linal is not a limiting factor for the proposed proton driver.
the present Linab is not limited by any of the components, and that a proton driver can be built using the present Linac.

the present Linal could be used as the first stage of the proposed proton driver with the following modifications: (a) a higher intensity source, (b) an improved beam extraction from the Linac into the Booster, and (c) an upgraded Booster.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the present Linal can accelerate beam at a current of 100 mA with beam loss of ~1.2%.
a Linac with a peak current in excess of 100 mA can be built with present technology.
the Linac can be operated at a peak current of ~85 mA and a pulse width of ~10 μsec.
